questions.text: This principle refers to the preparatory action that sets up and warns the audience of a bigger movement about to happen.
questions.hint: Think of a character crouching before a jump.

questions.text: An approach to drawing motion frame-by-frame in sequence from start to end, as opposed to planning only the key extreme poses first.
questions.answer: Straight Ahead Action and Pose to Pose
questions.hint: It's actually two contrasting animation workflows combined into one principle.

questions.text: This principle describes how parts of a body or object continue moving briefly after the main action stops, and how different parts move at different rates instead of stopping all at once.
questions.hint: Think of a character's hair or clothing still moving after they stop walking.

questions.text: This principle governs acceleration and deceleration in motion — more drawings/frames are placed near the start and end of an action, and fewer in the middle, so movement doesn't look mechanical.
questions.hint: CSS ease-in and ease-out timing functions mimic this principle.

questions.text: Almost all living, organic motion follows this kind of curved trajectory rather than a straight mechanical line.
questions.hint: Picture the natural curved swing of an arm or a pendulum.

questions.text: This principle refers to the number of frames or drawings used for an action, which determines the speed of the movement and communicates weight, mood, or emotion.
questions.hint: It's about how many frames an action takes, not the poses themselves.

questions.text: Which HTML tag creates the largest heading?
questions.hint: Heading tags are numbered from largest to smallest.

questions.text: What does CSS stand for?
questions.hint: The word 'Cascading' refers to how rules override one another.

questions.text: Which is the best practice for adding CSS to an HTML page?
questions.hint: This method keeps styling separate from content and is reusable across pages.

questions.text: In the CSS Box Model, which property controls space outside the element's border?
questions.hint: This is the outermost layer of the box model.

questions.text: Which animation principle states almost all living motion follows a curved path?
questions.hint: Think about the trajectory of a thrown ball.

questions.text: A character crouches before jumping. Which animation principle does this demonstrate?
questions.hint: It's the setup movement before the main action.

questions.text: Which animation principle do CSS ease-in and ease-out properties directly mimic?
questions.hint: This principle is about acceleration and deceleration of movement.

questions.text: Which design principle explains why a bright button stands out from surrounding body text?
questions.hint: This principle is about making one element visually different from the rest.

questions.text: The 60-30-10 rule is associated with which design principle?
questions.hint: This rule is about proportioning dominant, secondary, and accent hues.

questions.text: A web layout uses a 12-column invisible skeleton for consistent spacing. Which principle is this?
questions.hint: Think of the underlying structure many page layouts are built on.

questions.text: Which best describes a wireframe?
questions.hint: It's usually just boxes, lines, and placeholder text — no color or styling.

questions.text: What is the key difference between a mockup and a prototype?
options: Mockup has color; prototype does not
Mockup is interactive; prototype is static
Mockup is static; prototype is interactive
questions.hint: One of these can be clicked through; the other is just a still image.

questions.text: Which JavaScript method selects an element by ID and changes its content?
questions.hint: The method name directly references selecting by ID.

questions.text: Which design principle states: 'If it only works for some users, it isn't finished'?
questions.hint: This principle is about making sure everyone, including people with disabilities, can use the design.

questions.text: The most important animation principle — gives an object the illusion of weight and flexibility while keeping volume constant.
questions.hint: Think of a bouncing ball deforming as it hits the ground.

questions.text: Presents one clear focal point so the audience cannot miss the main idea; the silhouette reads instantly even in shadow.
questions.hint: It's about directing the viewer's attention to what matters most.

questions.text: A minor motion that adds richness without pulling focus from the main action — like a tail swishing while a character walks.
questions.hint: It supports the main action instead of competing with it.

questions.text: The animation principle referring to the overall quality that makes a character pleasant and interesting to watch, even a villain.
questions.hint: This is about charisma and visual interest, not necessarily being 'nice'.

questions.text: Related items placed close together; unrelated items given space — tells the viewer what belongs together without labels or borders.
questions.hint: It's about grouping through spacing.

questions.text: Reusing the same fonts, colors, and button styles throughout an interface so users only have to learn how something works once.
questions.hint: It's about consistency across the design.

questions.text: Generous empty space that improves readability and focus — the fastest way to make a design feel premium.
questions.hint: It's the empty area between and around elements.

questions.text: A high-fidelity, static design with full colors, real typography, and images — but no interactivity.
questions.hint: It looks like the finished product but you can't click through it.

questions.text: The CSS selector syntax used to target an element with a unique identifier (e.g., id="box").
questions.hint: It uses a special symbol placed right before the identifier's name.

questions.text: The stage in the design workflow that comes after a wireframe but before a prototype.
questions.hint: This stage adds visual polish but still isn't clickable yet.
